CITATION
:

Patrick v. St. Clair Catholic District School Board, 2013 ONSC 4025

COURT
FILE NO.:
1275/00 (Chatham)

DATE:
20130829

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

)

)

Jeffrey Patrick, Ann Patrick and
Chris Patrick

Plaintiffs

– and –

St. Clair Catholic District
School Board, Ray Power, Dianne Langan, Cindy Walker and Janey Mather
[1]

Defendants

)

) )

) )

) )

) ))))

Jerry F. O’Brien, for the Plaintiffs

Alex R. Szalkai and Josephine
Stark, for the Defendants

)

)

)

)

HEARD:
November 13, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20 and December 20, 2012

REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

Nolan j:

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This is an action for damages for personal
injury arising from an incident between Jeffrey Patrick (“Jeffrey”) and D.G. (“D.G.”)
that occurred in the schoolyard of St. Joseph’s School (“St. Joseph’s”) in
Tilbury, Ontario, on May 17, 2000, before the first class of the morning. A
group of grade 8 students, both boys and girls, were playing an informal game
of “keep-away” using a football. In accordance with the supervision plan in
place at the school during recess and other play times, two teachers were
assigned by the principal to supervise the schoolyard before classes began. In
the course of the game, D.G. pushed Jeffrey who fell to the ground. Jeffrey got
up, further pushes were exchanged, and Jeffrey fell again. The back of his head
hit the ground. D.G. then got on top of Jeffrey and punched him in the face a
number of times. Jeffrey suffered a brain injury. D.G. was charged as a young
offender and convicted of assault. Jeffrey never returned to St. Joseph’s
school after May 17, 2000.

[
2
]

Before proceeding with my judgment, I want to
express my gratitude to counsel for the professional way they conducted this
difficult trial. Their courtesy to one another, the witnesses and the court is
the hallmark of the true meaning of civility. At the same time, their courtesy
never diminished their vigorous advocacy on behalf of their respective clients.

[
3
]

At issue is the liability of the St. Clair
Catholic District School Board (“the Board”) and its personnel, specifically
the principal and vice principal of the School and the other named defendants
who were teachers at St. Joseph’s. The plaintiffs allege that the defendants owed
a duty of care to Jeffrey and that in failing to protect him from the injury by
D.G., they were negligent and breached their duties set out in the
Education
Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2, as amended, the regulations pursuant to the
Act
,
the
Occupiers Liability Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. O2 and the common law. The
quantum of damages is not in issue, having been agreed upon by the parties.

[
4
]

It is the position of the plaintiffs that the
Board and its personnel were negligent in three ways and that, but for the
Board’s negligence, the injury to Jeffrey would not have occurred. First, the
Board, principal and vice principal did not have an adequate plan of
supervision in place for the schoolyard, given its size, configuration and the
division of the schoolyard into three areas as well as a part of the school
property that was not visible from the back of the school and in which only
intermediate students could play with specific permission. Second, the level of
supervision provided by Mrs. Cindy Walker, the teacher assigned that day to
supervise the area where the assault took place fell below the standard of care
required in the circumstances. Third, the documented and undocumented incidents
involving breaches of school rules and the discipline code that came into
effect for the 1999 – 2000 school year by Jeffrey and D.G. should have resulted
in both of them being identified as students who required more than the usual
level of supervision in the schoolyard.

[
5
]

It is the position of the defendants that the
assault was a sudden and unexpected event that could not have been anticipated
by anyone and that the Board and its personnel were, thus, not negligent. The
defendants asserted that: Jeffrey and D.G. were cousins, their respective
parents considered them “the best of friends”, their parents allowed them to go
biking to playgrounds and other places unsupervised by adults, the incidents in
which Jeffrey and D.G. had been involved previously were “mischief” and,
because they had a “special relationship”, there was no need for special
supervision. Further, the plan of supervision for the schoolyard was adequate
and Mrs. Walker provided adequate supervision on the schoolyard that did not
fall below the standard of care.

[
6
]

For reasons below, I find that the plaintiffs
have failed to establish on the balance of probabilities that the defendants
breached their duty of care to Jeffrey and that his injury was the result of
their negligence. The action is, therefore, dismissed. In doing so, I echo the
poignant words of Lauwers J. in
Lee v. Toronto District School Board, et al.
,

2012 ONSC 3085, [2013] O.J. No. 1157
: “This is a hard and sad case, and I have
reached this conclusion only after long and anxious consideration.”

WITNESSES FOR THE PLAINTIFFS AND
DEFENDANTS

[
7
]

The witnesses for the plaintiffs were Mrs. Ann
Patrick, Jeffrey’s mother, and Mr. Michael McDonald, Mrs. Patrick’s partner and
Jeffrey’s stepfather since Jeffrey was two years old. In addition, D.G. and his
mother, K.G., testified for the plaintiffs. Mr. Stewart Toll was put forward as
an expert witness with respect to the adequacy of the supervision provided by
the school and schoolyard supervision. The defendants challenged both Mr.
Toll’s qualifications and the need to call him as an expert. A
voir dire

was held and I permitted Mr. Toll to testify with regard to supervisory and
policy practices related to schoolyard supervision as well as the adequacy and
appropriateness of the supervisory plan in place at St. Joseph’s school on May
17, 2000. I will have more to say later in this judgment about that evidence
and the basis on which I permitted Mr. Toll to testify.

[
8
]

The witnesses for the defendants were Mrs. Dianne
Langan, the vice principal of St. Joseph’s when the incident occurred, Mrs. Cindy
Walker, the teacher responsible for supervising the area of the playground
where the assault took place, on May 17, 2000, Mr. Raymond Power, the principal
of St. Joseph’s, Mrs. Jeanne Girard, who was the other teacher on playground
duty at the school that morning and Mrs. Janey Mather-Breault, Jeffrey’s seventh
grade teacher.

•

Exhibit 1 –
a school
layout brief which contained three copies of a drawing showing the
configuration of the schoolyard. This exhibit was used to explain the plan of
supervision in place at the time of the incident. It was also used by the
various witnesses to identify where they were at the time of the incident.

•

Exhibit 2
– a photograph
brief showing the layout of the schoolyard, with the location of various
significant areas related to the incident photographed from different angles.
This exhibit was also used by witnesses to mark the location of where they were
at the relevant times related to the incident.

•

Exhibits 3 to 8 inclusive –
Jeffrey and D.G.’s school records and incident reports, were made exhibits
by both the plaintiffs and defendants.

•

Exhibit 9 –
the hospital
record when Jeffrey attended the hospital because of an injury to his wrist
which occurred on September 15, 1999. He and D.G. were playing football in an
area of the schoolyard which was out of bounds to students because it is out of
the sight of the teachers supervising the schoolyard at the back of the school.

•

Exhibits 10 and 11
– D.G.’s statement to the police in June 2000, and the statement he
gave to an insurance adjuster some months later.

•

Exhibit 12
– the
Curriculum
Vitae
of Stewart Toll.

•

Exhibit 13
– a copy
of the read-ins at trial which were entered in written form with the consent of
both counsel. These read-ins contained certain admissions made at discovery by Mr.
James Arthur Clarke, the Superintendant of Education who was examined as a
representative of the Board, as well as certain portions of the discovery
evidence of Mr. Power, Mrs. Langan and Mrs. Walker.

•

Exhibit 14
– the letter
retaining Mr. Toll as an expert.

•

Exhibit 15
- the
Violence Free School Policy, dated June 15, 1999.

•

Exhibit 16
– a staff
meeting agenda, dated February 11, 2000.

•

Exhibit 17
- a
Principal’s Report, dated February 22, 2000.

•

Exhibit 18
- the
statement made by Mrs. Walker to an insurance adjuster, dated December 5, 2000.

[
9
]

In addition to the evidence presented at trial,
on November 16, 2012, I, along with counsel for both parties and a court
officer, attended at St. Joseph’s School for a “view” which is authorized by

rule 52.05
of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194. This
rule provides:

The judge or judge
and jury by whom an action is being tried or the court before whom an appeal is
being heard may, in the presence of the parties or their lawyers, inspect any
property concerning which any question arises in the action, or the place where
the cause of action arose.

The viewing
helped me to understand the layout diagrams and the photographs, as well as the
location of events central to this lawsuit.

[
10
]

In coming to my findings of fact and my ultimate
determination on the issue of liability, I have taken into account all of the
evidence that was presented. The fact that I may not make specific reference to
any part of the evidence during this judgment does not mean that it was not
considered by me in coming to my final determination.

BACKGROUND

a)

Jeffrey

[
11
]

The main plaintiff, Jeffrey, was born on April
9, 1987, and 25 years old at the time of trial. He had just turned 13 at the
time of the incident. He has an older brother, Chris, who is also one of the
plaintiffs by way of a
Family Law Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, claim. In
1992, Jeffrey started at St. Joseph’s in senior kindergarten. He had learning
difficulties for which he was tested in grade 2 and again in grade 4. His
mother obtained a tutor for him several times a week when he was in grade 4
which helped with his reading and his other learning needs. Jeffrey also
obtained significant help at the school from an occupational therapist, a
resource teacher and the use of a computer. While both Jeffrey and Mrs. Patrick
testified that all of these services provided by the school, as well as the
tutoring, helped Jeffrey with his school work and also his self-esteem, Jeffrey
continued to have learning and eventually behaviour issues at school. These
academic and behavioural issues are documented in various exhibits.

[
12
]

In grade 2, an Individual Educational Program
(“IEP”) was developed for Jeffrey which was adjusted from time to time while he
was at St. Joseph’s. The IEP prepared in grade 5 indicated that he had a mild
Central Auditory Problem (“CAP”) which resulted in Jeffrey having difficulty
understanding and following instructions.

[
13
]

During Jeffrey’s time at St. Joseph’s, Mrs.
Patrick, and sometimes Jeffrey’s stepfather, met regularly with the school
teachers and principal to deal with Jeffrey’s various learning and behavioural
issues at the school as well as teasing to which he and his parents alleged he
was regularly subjected.  In some of the reports in Exhibit 7, the school noted
that one of Jeffrey’s “strengths” was having supportive parents. The reports also
document a number of behaviour issues, including teasing, name calling and
physical aggression. They involved instances in which Jeffrey was a perpetrator
as well as a victim. Both Jeffrey and his mother acknowledged that he had anger
issues if he was picked on and that he sometimes started a confrontation in
those circumstances, as documented in his incident reports.

[
14
]

When Jeffrey was in grade five, Mrs. Patrick
complained to the principal that Jeffrey had been hit on the head with a ball
on purpose. Also in grade 5, Jeffrey complained about being followed home from
school by students in grade 8 and being pushed around by them before he left on
the bus or his bike for home. As a result, Mrs. Patrick picked up Jeffrey from
school for a while. Mrs. Patrick said that the police talked to the parents of
the children who had been “harassing” Jeffrey but nothing really changed. She
also complained to the school principal, but it was her view that the school
authorities never did anything to control the behaviour of the students who
were following him when he left the schoolyard.

[
15
]

Jeffrey continued to have problems in grade 6.
Some students called him names to the extent that Mrs. Patrick said it was
sometimes difficult to make him go to school. While the computer the school
obtained for him in grade 6 made a difference in Jeffrey’s abilities to keep up
with his school work, it also seemed to be a source of more teasing because it
seemed to make him appear more “different”.

[
16
]

Jeffrey had some friends at school including D.G.
who, at one point, Jeffrey considered to be his best friend. They had known
each other since they played hockey together in grade 1. Mrs. Patrick said they
were cousins, a fact that D.G.’s mother, K.G., disputed in her testimony. From
ages nine to 12, Jeffrey and D.G. were together a lot. They had sleepovers at
each other’s homes and fished and camped together. None of the parents saw
fights between them when they were at each other’s homes except for play wrestling.
Both Mrs. Patrick and K.G. testified that the two boys were allowed to go out
together on their bikes and go swimming without adult supervision. Outside of
school, they were considered independent and trustworthy by their parents.

b)

D.G.

[
17
]

D.G. was born on […], 1987, making him
12-years-old at the time of the assault on Jeffrey and 25-years-old when he
testified at trial. D.G.’s experiences at St. Joseph’s mirrored Jeffrey’s in
some respects. His School Records Brief, Exhibit 4, show him as being in grade
one in the 1993-1994 school year. By grade 3, his records reference some
behaviour and learning issues. In grade 5, his teacher commented that he had
difficulties completing homework but that his behaviour in class was “improving
greatly”. By the time he was in grade 7, he had an IEP in place. Comments in
that plan and in his progress reports referenced behaviour, learning, and
attention issues as confirmed by both D.G. and his mother, K.G.. Like Jeffrey,
he started to get teased in grade 5 “when I started getting heavier. Grade 6, I
was really heavy.”

[
18
]

When asked about the level of teasing he was
getting in grade seven, D.G. replied that “. . . it was pretty bad . . . . it
wasn’t just in school. It was out of school, at friends’ houses. It was just
everywhere I went.” The level of teasing did not change in grade 7. As to how
often it happened in that grade, he replied: “it was kind of the same really.
It wasn’t mostly just teasing. It was kind of everybody playing along with it
and it just became normal . . . to other people, not to me.”

[
19
]

Both K.G.  and D.G. testified that he told his
mother about the teasing. She talked to the school personnel but from her
perspective, nothing really changed. At one point, D.G. stood up in class when his
teacher, Mrs. McCann, was present and asked his grade seven classmates to stop
teasing him because he was “just tired of it. Figured if I say it in front of a
bunch of people, maybe they’ll understand more that I’m sick of it.” Nothing
really changed until grade 8 when he said the teasing seemed to stop.

[
20
]

D.G. was asked about the number of fights he had
been in at school before the May 17, 2000 incident in which he had used his
fists. His memory was that he was in grade three when he started “acting up and
thinking I was a little macho whatever.” He thought he was in five or six fights
in which he used his fists before the day of the incident.

[
21
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs reviewed his incident
reports with D.G. in grade 7, Exhibit 3. D.G. did not remember two incidents in
October when he broke a thermos and when he took something chocolate from
another student’s lunch. He had some recollection of the incident in November when
he and others were throwing rocks at a light in the gymnasium, and of being
suspended as a result. He did not remember an incident in which he and some
others were wrestling in the schoolyard but acknowledged that wrestling was
something he and others like to do. He knew that it was prohibited at school
but he and others still did it. D.G. also did not remember a schoolyard
incident written up by Mrs. Walker in which he and Jeffrey were throwing stones
at girls but said Mrs. Walker was a strict playground supervisor and would
impose consequences like walking with her for recess “if she caught you
breaking the rules.”

[
22
]

With respect to his relationship with Jeffrey, D.G.
said they met at school. It was D.G.’s evidence that, although he and Jeffrey
were friends and “hung out after school a few times before the fight”, Jeffrey
was not his closest friend. It was his recollection that he and Jeffrey did not
hang out much after school when they were in grade 7. D.G. was not sure if he
and Jeffrey were ever in the same class.

[
23
]

D.G. was also questioned about the incident with
Jeffrey in the washroom on May 13, 2000, just four days before the event that
led to this trial. While he did not have a clear recollection of the event, he
thought from the contents of the incident report that he had left an assembly
and went to the washroom without permission. D.G. was not sure what “Strike
Two” written on the report meant but said there was a point system in class for
behaviour where students who accumulated too many points would not be permitted
to go on the year end field trip.

[
24
]

Interestingly, D.G. had no recollection of the
September 1999 incident with Jeffrey in which Jeffrey sprained his wrist.

[
25
]

When asked about his memory of Mrs. Walker when
she was on schoolyard duty, he said: “She’d patrol the area, watch the kids,
make sure everything was good and everyone was safe and kids were doing the
right thing.”

[
26
]

D.G. was also asked for his view of Mrs. Walker
as a classroom teacher. He responded in the affirmative to suggestions put to
him that she would deal with problems, explain to the student why he or she
should not act in a particular way, she was firm and did not “put up with
things in the class.”

[
27
]

D.G. also responded affirmatively when asked by
counsel if there were rules at the school about “hands off”, “no deliberate
pushing”, “no fighting” and “no wrestling, even WFF (sic) style.” D.G.
acknowledged that in spite of the rule, they did wrestle “on and off”. He went
on to say: “If we chose to do it, we’d make sure that the teachers would –
backs would be turned or we’d try our best to avoid teachers.” D.G. also said
that teasing was forbidden and when he was being teased he really did not want
help from the teachers or his mother and he definitely did not want to tell on
anyone because that person or persons would get in trouble.

[
28
]

Although D.G. seemed to downplay the effect of
the teasing on him, K.G. considered that the teasing was a “very serious”
problem for D.G. and that “he was very hurt by it.” She said that she had
talked to either D.G.’s teacher, Mrs. McCann or Mr. Power about the issue.  She
said she thought “the school board, the teachers at the school knew it was
going on and they were trying to handle it as best they could.”

c)

The 1999 – 2000 School Year

[
29
]

In September 1999, Jeffrey started in grade 7 in
a split grade 6 and 7 class. D.G. was in an all-grade 7 class. Jeffrey’s
teacher was a first-year teacher, Janey Mather-Breault, one of the defendants
who testified at the trial. By that fall, Jeffrey weighed 110 pounds, 20 pounds
more than what he weighed in grade six. Other students including D.G. teased
him about being fat. D.G. was also teased about being fat by other students,
including Jeffrey. D.G.’s teacher was Mrs. McCann.

[
30
]

On September 15, 1999, Jeffrey suffered a
sprained hand when he and D.G. were playing football in the area of the school
property off limits to students except with specific permission. They either
ran into each other or D.G. pushed him in an attempt to get the ball. Jeffrey
agreed, either way, it was accidental. He had a cast on his hand for six weeks
and had to be driven to and from school. Mr. McDonald was called to the school
that day to take Jeffrey for medical treatment. Jeffrey and D.G. stopped
spending time together outside of school after September 1999 when they were in
different classrooms and Jeffrey’s wrist was injured. There was no incident or
accident report prepared by any school personnel documenting the incident.

[
31
]

Jeffrey and his mother both said that the
teasing to which he was subject was not restricted to the schoolyard. Jeffrey
complained to his mother about being mistreated by other students in the
classroom. He said he had markers thrown at him and was stabbed in the back by
other students with a protractor in November or December, 1999 leaving puncture
marks on his back that were seen by both Mrs. Patrick and Mr. McDonald. Jeffrey
also said he had two yardsticks broken over his back by the same students. They
both said he had welts on his back. Mrs. Patrick contacted Mr. Power about the
protractor incident but was not satisfied with how either Jeffrey’s teacher or
Mr. Power dealt with the problem. She said it took four weeks for Jeffrey to be
moved to a different seat in the classroom, in spite of her complaints.
Jeffrey, however, said he had been moved in two days and I accept his evidence
on that issue.

[
32
]

Mrs. Patrick said that she also spoke with Mr.
Power about the yardsticks that were broken over Jeffrey’s back. He said he
would check into it and call her back but she said he never did. Ms.
Mather-Breault had no recollection of these or any other classroom incidents
involving Jeffrey being picked on by other students in her classroom. No
incident reports were prepared by her documenting the incidents but Mr. Power
recalled discussing some of those issues with her.

[
33
]

The minutes of the February 24, 2000 IEP meeting,
which Mrs. Patrick attended with school personnel, indicate that the school
personnel recommended considering a behaviour/academic contract if Jeffrey’s
behaviour issues continued. A review was to take place after March break. A
behaviour/academic contract was not put in place although Jeffrey received a two-day
suspension after the March break for kicking another student, Raymond Reaume on
March 23, 2000 during an incident on the schoolyard.

[
34
]

On May 13, 2000, four days before the incident
at issue in the trial, there was an incident involving D.G. and Jeffrey in the
boy’s washroom. According to Jeffrey, he had been in the washroom first and D.G.
came in and pushed him into the urinal. According to D.G.’s note, he said
Jeffrey pushed him first and he pushed back. When Jeffrey was asked why there
were two different versions of the same incident, Jeffrey responded: “Well, you
won’t sell yourself out, will you?”

[
35
]

Mrs. Patrick said she called Mr. Power about the
incident to ask him to take some action. She said she was surprised by the
incident because it had been her understanding that Jeffrey had stayed away
from D.G. after the sprained hand incident in September 1999. Also, they were
in different classrooms so she thought their direct contact was reduced.

THE INCIDENT – May 17, 2000

(a)

The Location

[
36
]

For the school year beginning in September 1999,
St. Joseph’s had an enrolment of approximately 425 students, ranging from
junior kindergarten to grade 8. The schoolyard behind the school building is
approximately 300 feet deep and almost 560 feet wide. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain
scale drawings of the yard as well as photographs of the play area taken from
various angles. The sight lines are clear and unobstructed except for an area
behind the gymnasium which cannot be seen from the back of the school. Grade 7
and 8 students were allowed to play on the basketball pad located there with
permission. Otherwise, that area was off limits to students playing in the schoolyard
before and after school as well as at recess and lunch times.

[
37
]

The student body was divided into three groups:
students in kindergarten and in grades one to three were in the primary group
and assigned to the left side of the playground as it appears in Exhibit 1.
Students in grades four to six were in the junior group and assigned to the
middle area of the playground. Students in grades seven and eight were in the
intermediate group and assigned to the right side of the playground.

[
38
]

In spite of there being these three divisions,
for supervision purposes, the playground was divided into two parts with “an
imaginary line” down the middle. There were two teachers on playground duty
before school and at the two recesses of the day. There was also supervision
over the lunch hour and for a period after school. The principal, with the
assistance of the vice principal, assigned these yard duties to all teachers on
a rotating basis. In addition to the two teachers, both Mr. Power and Mrs.
Langan testified that each of them also frequently went out on the playground
as a way of getting to know the children. Neither of them was in the schoolyard
before class on May 17, 2000.

[
39
]

The incident between Jeffrey and D.G. took place
on the grassy area depicted on page 2 of Exhibit 1, located approximately 150
feet past the asphalt pad also marked on that diagram. On the day of the
assault, Mrs. Walker was the teacher assigned to supervise the half of the
playground assigned to part of the junior group and the intermediate group.

[
40
]

Although the enrolment of the school was
approximately 425 students, there would have been fewer students on the
playground at the time of the incident. Mr. Power as well as Mrs. Walker estimated
the number to be no more than 300. This is because the kindergarten students
only attend alternate days, the junior kindergarten students go directly into
their classroom, the grade 8 students are permitted to go into their classrooms
prior to the commencement of the first class and other students are involved in
the breakfast program in various capacities.

(b)

The Players

[
41
]

The only eye-witness evidence about the incident
came from Jeffrey and D.G.. Other evidence came from Mr. Power, the principal.
Although neither he nor any of the other teachers witnessed the incident, Mr.
Power conducted an investigation after the incident for the purposes of
completing a report to the Board as he was required to do. In the course of
that investigation, he spoke with three other students who were present at the
time of the assault and he noted their observations in his report. Both Mrs.
Patrick and K.G. testified about their knowledge of the events after they had
been called by the school and picked up their respective sons. The following is
the evidence of each of the players with respect to the incident itself.

i)

Jeffrey

[
42
]

According to Jeffrey, on May 17, 2000, he rode
his bike to school, arriving at approximately 8:35 a.m. The school bell did not
ring until 8:55 a.m. and Jeffrey came to school early anticipating the
opportunity to play with friends and school mates before class began. When he
arrived, a group of grade seven boys and girls, (according to Jeffrey more
girls than boys), were engaged in a game of “keep-away” using a football on the
grassy area of the yard beyond the asphalt. The game consisted of the boys
trying to keep the ball away from the girls. D.G. was one of the participants.

[
43
]

After playing for a bit, Jeffrey said that the
players started getting rough. When asked what that meant, the following
exchange took place:

A.

They were starting to push to get the ball.

Q.  And were people
missing the ball when it was thrown to them?

A.  That’s why you
were getting pushed, so you would miss the ball.

Q.  . . .and, what
would happen if you’d missed the ball?

A.  You’d get
pushed more.

[
44
]

Jeffrey went on to say that the pushing went on
for two or three minutes. Then, more students showed up to play and “the
atmosphere changed.” Swearing started and anyone who missed catching the ball
would get sworn at loudly by the other players.

[
45
]

Jeffrey said both swearing and pushing were
prohibited behaviours at the school so he looked around to see if a teacher was
watching because “What we were doing wasn’t really by the rules.” He said he
did not see a teacher. He said the swearing went on for two or three minutes.

[
46
]

Jeffrey said that after he had played for about
10 minutes, he was “just standing there” and someone threw the ball to him and
he missed it. He said that D.G. then pushed him, using two hands on his chest
and he fell down “on my butt.” Jeffrey got up and pushed D.G. but he did not
fall down. D.G. pushed him back and Jeffrey fell backwards and the back of his
head hit ground with “a hard thud.” Jeffrey thought he might have been knocked
out. He said that when “I got feeling back and he was on top of me, hitting me,
so I grabbed his hand to stop him from hitting me in the face.” Jeffrey
estimated that from the time he was on the ground the second time, he got his
feeling back and he realized that D.G. was on top of him hitting him, a couple
of minutes had passed.

[
47
]

Jeffrey said that while he was lying on his
back, D.G. was straddling him, sitting on his stomach with both of Jeffrey’s
arms pinned under D.G.’s legs. D.G. hit him at least five to 10 times in the
face. Jeffrey said he struggled to get his hands free from under D.G.’s legs
and when he did, he grabbed both of D.G.’s hands. It was then that “something
hit me on the top of the head.” He described the hit as feeling like a hard
thud but he knew it did not come from D.G.. Jeffrey said “Everything went black.”
He went on to describe that when he got “feeling back” and got up, saw he was
bleeding and saw D.G. to the right of him. D.G. then left and when he returned,
about two minutes later, he had Kleenex with him. Jeffrey assumed that D.G. had

required of boards of education, principals, and teachers with respect to plans
of supervision and the execution of those plans as well as to opine about the

qualifications and that his evidence was not necessary. A
voir dire
was
held.

[

Mr. Toll is president of Exemplary Consultants
(London) Ltd. (“Exemplary”), a company that was formed in 1988. The company
provides consulting and counselling services to individuals, school boards and
governments on educational issues, as well as expert reports and evidence to
lawyers dealing with education cases, including liability issues.

[
73
]

Mr. Toll began his teaching career in 1957 and
progressed through the hierarchy of the education system in various parts of
the southwest region of Ontario, but primarily with the Middlesex County Board
of Education until his retirement in December 1987 from that board as Director
of Education and Secretary of the Board.

[
74
]

Prior to serving as Director of Education, he
served as Assistant Director of Education, Superintendent of Development and
Special Education, Superintendent of Special Programs and Area Superintendent.
From 1962 to 1966 and again from 1968 to 1969, Mr. Toll was a professor at the
Windsor Teachers College where his duties involved teaching and supervising
student teachers. In addition to teaching English, child development, and
educational psychology, he taught general methodology including schoolyard supervision.

[

I had a number of concerns about Mr. Toll’s
qualification as an expert called to express an opinion about the adequacy of
the schoolyard supervision plan in place at St. Joseph's at the time of the
incident.  First, his experience is not current, having retired from the school
system almost 25 years ago. Although as the president of Exemplary Consultants
he has been involved in professional development of teachers and principals
since that time, his on-the-job experience was dated. Second, his letter of
engagement by plaintiffs’ counsel, which was accompanied by a copy of the Trial
Record, both the plaintiffs' and defendants' affidavits of documents, medical
briefs, the transcripts of all of the examinations for discovery and the school
records of both Jeffrey and D.G., requested his opinion as to whether “the
school board and/or it's (sic) various employees breached their duty of care in
a manner that was causally related to Jeffrey Patrick being injured”, the
question for the court to determine. In my view, such a request was unfortunate
as it invites the proposed expert to view the accompanying materials from a
perspective of blame, rather than from an objective perspective which is
expected of experts, particularly since the change in the
Rules of Civil
Procedure

regarding experts, the result of the Osborne Report of November,
2007.

]

Despite these concerns, I qualified Mr. Toll to
testify as an expert with respect to schoolyard supervisory policies and
practice and also the appropriateness and adequacy of the supervision plan in
place at the school on May 17, 2000. In coming to that conclusion I applied the
four part test set out in
R. v. Mohan
,
1994 CanLII 80 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 9. On the basis
of the evidence of Mr. Toll on the
voir dire
, I was satisfied that understanding
the rules for ensuring child safety in a schoolyard requires more than the

principles underlying the development of a plan of supervision which Mr. Toll
has gained as a result of practical experience and teaching those principles to
others, including principals and teachers.

[
77
]

I was also mindful of the practical approach
expressed by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Alfano (Trustee of) v. Piersanti
,

2012 ONCA 297
, [2012] No. O.J. 2042 with respect to the qualification of an
expert in cases where the disqualification of the proposed expert could have a
serious effect on the case of the party proposing the expert as set out at
paragraph 111 of the decision:

In most cases, the
issue of whether an expert lacks independence or objectivity is addressed as a
matter of weight to be attached to the expert’s evidence rather than as a
matter of the admissibility. Typically, when such an attack is mounted, the
court will admit the evidence and weigh it in light of the independence
concerns. Generally, admitting the evidence will not only be the path of least
resistance, but also accord with common sense and efficiency.

THE LAW

Introduction

[
200
]

There was no serious dispute between the parties
that both pursuant to the
Education Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2, as well as
the regulations thereto and the common law, boards of education and their staff
owe a duty of care to students, both in the school and on the schoolyard during
official school hours. There was also no dispute that a board of education and
its personnel are not insurers against accidents that occur in the school or on
the schoolyard where there is no negligence or breach of the standard of care.
The standard of care is recognized to be that of a prudent and reasonable
parent. The burden is on the plaintiffs to establish on a balance of
probabilities that the defendants breached that duty and, as a result of that
breach, Jeffrey was injured.

Statutes and Regulations

[
201
]

The obligation of teachers with respect to
discipline and supervision is set out in
s. 264(1)
(e) of the
Education Act
:

To maintain, under
the direction of the principal, proper order and discipline in the teacher’s
classroom and while on duty in the school and on the school ground;

[
202
]

In Regulation 298 passed pursuant to the
Education
Act
, the duties of teachers with respect to discipline is further expanded
in s. 20:

(b)   carry out supervision duties and instructional program assigned
to teacher by principal;

...

(g)  ensure
that all reasonable safety procedures are carried out in courses and activities
for which the teacher is responsible;....

[
203
]

With respect to the obligations of principals in
regard to discipline, they are set out in
s. 265(1)
of the
Education Act
:

It is the duty of a
principal of a school, in addition to the principal’s duties as a teacher,

(a)

to maintain proper order and discipline in the school;

...

(i)  to furnish
to the Ministry and to the appropriate supervisory officer any information that
it may be in the principal’s power to give respecting the condition of the
school premises, the discipline of the school, the progress of the pupils and
any other matter affecting the interests of the school, and to prepare such
reports for the board as are required by the board;

(j)    to give
assiduous attention to the health and comfort of the pupils....

[

]

Further, in Regulation 298, s. 11, the relevant

(1)

(a)

the instruction and the discipline of pupils in the school; and

(b)

the organization and management of the school.

...

(3)   In addition to the duties under the Act and those assigned by

...

]

Case Law

[
208
]

I was referred to a number of cases by both
counsel for the plaintiffs and for the defendants in support of their
respective positions.

[
209
]

In
Myers v. Peel County Board of Education
,

1981 CanLII 27 (SCC)
, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 21, a student attempting a difficult dismount after working on
rings in the gymnasium fell and broke his neck. The trial judge found that the
supervision was inadequate given the student’s age, the circumstances under
which the incident occurred and the nature of the activity engaged in. The
Ontario Court of Appeal had allowed the appeal, finding that there was no evidence
that more mats on the gymnasium floor would have avoided the injury and that it
could not be assumed that a teacher’s presence would have avoided the accident.

[
210
]

McIntyre J. writing for the Supreme Court of
Canada granted the appeal and restored the finding of the trial judge. On p. 31
of that decision, McIntyre J. said:

The standard of care
to be exercised by school authorities in providing for the supervision and
protection of students for whom they are responsible is that of the careful or
prudent parent, described in
Williams v. Eady

(1895), 10 T.L.R. 41
. It
has, no doubt, become somewhat qualified in modern times because of the greater
variety of activities conducted in schools, with probably larger groups of
students using more complicated and more dangerous equipment than formerly: see

McKay et al. v. The Board of the Govan School Unit No. 29 of Saskatchewan et
al.
,
1968 CanLII 76 (SCC)
, [1968] S.C.R. 589, but with the qualification expressed in the
McKay

case and noted by Carruthers J.A. in
Thornton, supra,
it remains the
appropriate standard for such cases. It is not, however, a standard which can
be applied in the same manner and to the same extent in every case. Its
application will vary from case to case and will depend upon the number of
students being supervised at any given time, the nature of the exercise or
activity in progress, the age and the degree of skill and training which the
students may have received in connection with such activity, the nature and
condition of the equipment in use at the time, the competency and capacity of
the students involved, and a host of other matters which may be widely varied
but which, in a given case, may affect the application of the prudent
parent-standard to the conduct of the school authority in the circumstances.

[
211
]

Starting at p. 35 of the same decision, McIntyre
J. went on to say:

As to the absence of
supervision, again I am not prepared to accept the proposition advanced by the
respondent that the presence of a teacher supervising at the time of the
accident would not have prevented the accident, nor that it is incumbent upon
the appellant to prove that the presence of the teacher would have prevented
the accident. On a balance of all the probabilities it was the opinion of the
trial judge, which in my view of the evidence was justified, that the absence
of supervision contributed to the cause of the accident. In my opinion, it
cannot be said that the presence of a teacher among six to eight students in
the exercise room would not have had a restraining effect upon the students
which could have influenced the course of events and prevented the accident.
The respondent should have anticipated reckless behaviour from at least some of
the young boys sent off by themselves to work on gymnastic equipment. The
evidence revealed that it was a recurring problem to keep students from
attempting gymnastic exercises without spotters and the proclivity of young
boys of high school age to act recklessly in disregard, if not in actual
defiance, of authority is, as was pointed out by Blair J.A. in dissent in the
Court of Appeal, well known. It cannot be an answer here for the school
authorities to say as they did that even the presence of a supervising teacher
would not have prevented the accident.

[
212
]

In
Hentze (Guardian of) v. Campbell River
School District No. 72
,
1994 CanLII 173 (BC CA)
, [1994] B.C.J. No. 1876, 49 B.C.A.C. 241, the
British Columbia Court of Appeal considered the appeal of the decision of a
trial judge who found a school teacher negligent in the discharge of her duties
for failing to properly supervise students who were engaged in play fighting
during lunch. A seven-year-old boy was rough housing with some bigger boys and
sustained an injury. The teacher testified that she was talking with some other
children and had stood with her back to the part of the playground where the
children were playing.

[
213
]

The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal by the
school board. Writing for that court Finch J.A. said, at para. 7:

This sequence of events, as I understand the line of reasoning which I
attribute to the judge, could not all have taken place within the one minute,
or less, that the teacher says elapsed from the time of her observation of the
area.  Several minutes would have been necessary.  The teacher's time
estimate was mistaken because she was distracted by the discussion in which she
became engaged with the children at the front of the school.

[
214
]

Further, at para. 9, Finch J.A. said:

I am inclined to agree with the appellant, when it says that the
evidence does not establish a period of non-observation of the subject area for
at least five minutes.  However, without assigning a specific number of
minutes to the elapsed time, I conclude that the judge did not err when he
inferred that the “rough housing” had continued for several minutes, and for a
period of time “long enough that it ought to have been observed by a teacher
responsible for supervision of the whole of the play area.”

[
215
]

At paras. 14 and 15, Finch J.A. said:

The law does not, of
course, require that school authorities keep students under constant
supervision at all times.  The standard is that of the reasonably careful
and prudent parent.  How the standard is to be applied in any given case
will depend upon many factors, including the nature and size of the area to be
supervised, the number and ages of the students involved, and the nature of the
activity or activities that are in progress.

Having regard for
all of the circumstances here, and for the appellant's own policies with
respect to supervision, I am not persuaded that the learned trial judge erred
in concluding that the appellant fell below the applicable standard of care.

]

1996 CanLII 237 (SCC)
, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825. That case

,
2012 ONSC 3085

In regard to the issue of whether the second

[
244

The OSR card for grade one reported him being

ANALYSIS

Plaintiffs’ Position

[
247
]

As set out in their trial memorandum at paras.
17 and 18, the plaintiffs urged me to find:

17.       Given the
large number of students to be supervised, the size of the yard with hidden
areas, the dangers inherent in a game of keep away between grade 7 girls and
boys, the history of Jeff and D.G. and their learning disabilities, the length
of time that the altercation between Jeff and D.G. involved, the plaintiffs
submit that the defendants breached their duty of care including in the
following ways:

i.

Cindy Walker failed to follow the yard
supervision policy that was in place;

ii.

The principal’s plan for supervision was
inadequate for the number of students, the size of the yard and the site lines
that existed;

iii.

The teachers including Ms. Mathers failed to
document the incidents involving Jeff Patrick while he was in her class; Jeff
and D.G. should have been identified for extra monitoring during the recess;
the board supervisor, James Clark, failed to ensure that St. Joseph’s school
plan of supervision and identification of behaviour and discipline issues was
adequate.

18.  But for the
defendants breach of their duty of care, Jeff would not have been assaulted.

Defendants’ Position

[
248
]

It was the position of the defendants that the
Board and the school personnel including Mrs. Walker acted in accordance with
their duties to provide adequate supervision to all the students in their care,
supervision that would be provided by a careful and prudent parent. It was
further the defendants’ position that the evidence of the plaintiffs did not
establish otherwise on the balance of probabilities. Counsel argued that:

1)

Mr. Power, acting under his responsibilities as
principal to carry out the policies of the Board, including the Violence Free
Schools Policy of June 1999, Exhibit 15, put in place a plan of supervision
that met the Board’s and his obligations. The plan of supervision for the schoolyard
was communicated to the teachers along with the schedule and reinforced at
regular staff meetings;

2)

neither Jeffrey or D.G. were “high risk”
students who needed a higher level of supervision;

3)

Mrs. Walker, as an experienced teacher, was
familiar with her obligations when she was on schoolyard supervision and
carried out those obligations in an appropriate manner;

4)

when the plan of supervision was changed to
three teachers in the fall of 2000, the change was because of a new requirement
by the Board and OSBIE, the insurance company that a teacher be at the
playground equipment at all times.

APPLICATION OF THE LAW

[
249
]

Applying the principles espoused in the case law
to the facts before me, I will address each of the allegations of negligence raised
by the plaintiffs.

Plan of Supervision and the Alleged Negligence of Mrs. Walker

[
250
]

I am satisfied on the basis of the evidence of
Mr. Power, Mrs. Langan and the other teachers, including Mrs. Walker, that St.
Joseph’s had an adequate plan of supervision for the schoolyard during the
period before the first class of the day. Although the enrolment of the school
in the 1999 – 2000 year was approximately 425, I accept the evidence of Mr.
Power and the other witnesses who confirmed that for reasons I have set out
earlier in this judgment there were approximately 300 students in the schoolyard
most mornings before class and the morning of May 17, 2000 was no exception. I
also accept the evidence of Ms. Girard, the other teacher on schoolyard duty
with Mrs. Walker that day that the playground equipment was off limits to all
students before class in the morning. Whether two teachers were sufficient at
other recess times during the day is not an issue I need to determine. The
incident giving rise to this trial occurred during the time before the first
class in the morning.

[
251
]

I also find that Mr. Power had given
consideration to the appropriate number of teachers required to supervise the schoolyard.
When he first came to St. Joseph’s as a teaching vice principal, there was only
one teacher on schoolyard supervision. He considered the size of the yard and
the number of students and recommended to the principal that the number of
supervisory teachers be increased to two. The principal at that time accepted
his recommendation and implemented the change. There was no evidence that the
enrolment of St. Joseph’s had increased significantly or at all since that
time.

[
252
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs pointed to the
increase in the number of supervising teachers from two to three for the 2000 –
2001 school year. Mr. Power and the other witnesses for the defendants all said
that the reason for the increase was because of new directions from the Board
and possibly OSBIE, the insurance company that insures boards of education that
provided that there had to be one supervisor in attendance at the playground
equipment at all times. I have no reason to doubt that evidence in spite of the
argument of plaintiffs’ counsel that there was no “paper” to confirm the
directive.

[
253
]

At her discovery, Mrs. Langan said that she and
other teachers recommended to Mr. Power that the number of teachers on the
playground be increased to three from two. She said this was because of the
size of the yard and the number of students to supervise. It was not clear,
however, that her recommendation in that regard was related in any way to this
incident or was in relation to one teacher having to remain at all times by the
playground equipment.

[
254
]

The law is clear that subsequent remedial
measures are not, standing on their own to be taken as an admission of
liability. They can be considered along with all of the other evidence relevant
to liability (
Sandhu (Litigation Guardian of) v. Wellington Place Apartments
,

2008 ONCA 215
).

[
255
]

Even if a plan of supervision is adequate and
meets the standard of care, execution of that plan can fall below the standard
of care. The evidence of Mr. Power, Mrs. Langan, Mrs. Walker and the other
teachers who testified, along with the read-in from the discovery of Mr.
Clarke, the Superintendant of Education, all stressed the need for the teachers
to circulate around the schoolyard and be visible to the students. At his
discovery, Mr. Clarke was asked about the position of the Board’s Violence Free
School policy dealing with promoting safety which provides: “Staff is visible
and the Principal organizes supervision.” Mr. Clarke answered: “I would say to
act as a deterrent if students were contemplating any misdeed, that staff being
visible would be a deterrent to that.”

[
256
]

Similarly at his discovery, Mr. Power made it
clear that the number of teachers assigned to supervise was based in part on
their visibility on the schoolyard, that their presence and visibility can
deter inappropriate conduct, that these instructions and expectations were
communicated to teachers through staff meetings: “We would talk about moving
around, making sure that they covered areas through the yard, to identify areas
of concern, be it rough play or congregations of students that might cause
concern that something might be happening . . . We could talk about being
proactive, trying to be in locations before things developed.”

[
257
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs urged me to find that
Mrs. Walker’s supervision of the schoolyard that day fell below the standard of
care. He urged me to find that Mrs. Walker was not circulating through her part
of the yard and that she may not even have been on the yard, as Jeffrey said he
looked for a teacher and did not see one. Rather, he saw Mrs. Walker coming out
of the junior doors after he had been assaulted and was standing up again.
Jeffrey also said that there had been pushing and shoving among the
participants in the game of keep-away for several minutes before D.G. ran into
him, pushing him down. If Jeffrey’s evidence is correct, this would establish
that there were activities taking place that should have been noticed by Mrs.
Walker, causing her to step in and take charge of the situation in a pro-active
manner.

[
258
]

In my view, Jeffrey’s evidence like the evidence
of all witnesses must be closely scrutinized in relation to its reliability. I
have no doubt that Jeffrey was doing his best to tell the truth about how he
remembered the events of May 17, 2000. It is not his credibility that is in
issue, it is the reliability of his evidence that raises serious doubts. In
Rollins
,
E. Ducharme J. set out a helpful explanation of the difference between
credibility and reliability at paras. 47-50. I rely on and adopt that analysis
as I consider Jeffrey’s evidence. I do not accept his evidence that there was
pushing and swearing for a number of minutes before D.G. ran into him and the
fight started. None of the statements given to Mr. Power by Kevin Key, Brendon
Bartlett or Derek Patrick can be taken to support that evidence. Even Jeffrey
admitted on cross-examination that if someone looked over at the game and
observed the play, that person would have no reason to be concerned.

[
259
]

I also do not accept Jeffrey’s evidence that he
saw Mrs. Walker come out of the junior doors after the fight was over.

[
260
]

Another reason to doubt the reliability of
Jeffrey’s evidence is his insistence that in addition to being hit in the face
and head by D.G., he was kicked in the head by some unknown person, “clothes
lined” by Kevin Key and Brendon Bartlett, and hit in the face by Derek Patrick.
Even though Jeffrey said that he testified under oath at D.G.’s trial that he
was “clothes lined” by them and K.G. recalled that testimony, I would need to
review the transcript of the trial to understand how that statement would have
been relevant to the issue of whether D.G. was guilty of an assault against
Jeffrey. Jeffrey had no explanation of why he did not tell Mr. Power about
those incidents when Mr. Power spoke to him to get his version of the events.
Jeffrey’s insistence that those incidents took place cause me to further
question the reliability of his evidence in general.

[
261
]

I accept Mrs. Walker’s evidence that she never
left the yard. Her oral evidence is supported by her notes about other
incidents she dealt with that morning. I also accept her evidence that she
circulated around the yard, and she was aware of the game of keep-away going on
with the football. Mrs. Girard also saw her circulating on the yard. While Mrs.
Girard was responsible for a different part of the schoolyard, the whole of the
yard except for the part behind the gym can be seen from anywhere in the yard.
There are no obstructions. Mrs. Girard saw nothing in any part of the yard to
cause her concern.

[
262
]

I accept D.G.’s evidence about how the incident
took place. The game involved the boys passing the ball around to keep the
girls from getting it and trying to get it back from them if they got it. I
accept that D.G. ran into Jeffrey accidently and that push set in place a chain
of events that ended up with Jeffrey being seriously injured. I accept that the
whole episode was as D.G. described it: “bing, bang, boom done.” While it
lasted longer than five or ten seconds as suggested by defendants’ counsel, I
find it lasted less than one minute. The aftermath lasted longer than the
event.

[
263
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs urged me to find that
if Mrs. Walker was where she said she was that it was inconceivable that she
did not see D.G. running into the school and back out with Kleenex for Jeffrey.
Counsel for the defendants urged me to find that D.G. never went into the
school. I accept D.G.’s evidence that he did. There were approximately 300
children playing on the schoolyard that morning. To see a child running in the schoolyard
would not catch one’s attention. I do not find that this is evidence of
negligence on Mrs. Walker’s part.

[
264
]

All the cases to which I was referred by both
counsel espouse the following principle: what is expected of school boards and
their personnel in relation to their duty of care to their students is that
they act as careful and prudent parents. There is nothing inherently dangerous
in a game of keep-away. It is not an activity like gymnastics or even tackle
football that would require a higher level of supervision. A careful and
prudent parent would have no hesitation in permitting his or her child to play
the game.

[
265
]

In
Hentze
, the British Columbia Court of
Appeal upheld the findings of the trial judge in which he found a school
district liable on account of the negligence of a teacher supervising a
playground and failed to prevent an accident that occurred when a seven year
old was play fighting with some older children. Unfortunately, the trial
decision was not available and the complete rendition of the facts was not set
out in the decision of the Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal did say,
however, that the teacher who was supposed to be supervising the part of the
yard where the accident occurred was engaged for several minutes “at the front
of the school” talking with some other students with her back to the yard. The
trial judge also found that the rough-housing had continued for several
minutes. Those facts can be distinguished from the facts in the case before me
as I have found that the whole incident from the time D.G. ran into Jeffrey
until they were both on their feet and Jeffrey had a bloody nose lasted less
than one minute.

[
266
]

I also cannot find on the evidence I accept that
having more supervisors in the schoolyard would have prevented the incident. It
was a sudden, unexpected event in the midst of an acceptable, safe activity, an
activity that Jeffrey’s and D.G.’s parents would have permitted them to play.
Indeed, both Mrs. Patrick and K.G. testified that Jeffrey and D.G. were able to
engage in activities such as going to the park or going “downtown” on their own
without any adult supervision.

[
267
]

In the Statement of Claim, the plaintiffs
asserted that the accident happened “suddenly”. I am satisfied that the
evidence at trial supports this assertion. This assertion also supports Mrs.
Walker’s evidence that she did not see any out of the ordinary behaviour on the
part of the group playing keep-away leading up to the assault.

Were Jeffrey and/or D.G. “High Risk” Students requiring a Higher
Level of Supervision?

[
268
]

I find that the plaintiffs have failed to
establish on the balance of probabilities that neither Jeffrey or D.G. were “high
risk” students. They both had special learning needs that were being addressed
by the school. Their respective incident reports reflected a number of
occasions when each of them, together or individually, broke the school rules
that they each testified they were well aware of. Those incidents, even taken
together, were not sufficiently serious for the school to conclude that either
Jeffrey or D.G. or both of them could be identified as students who were a risk
to others, thus earning them the label of being “high risk”. The school had a
system in place to identify “high risk” students. Those were students who were
“high risk” on account of their academic needs and were at risk of not being
successful academically. The other category of “high risk” student was a
student who was at risk of hurting themselves or of hurting others. Several
students who fell into the latter category were referred to during the trial.
Plans were put in place by the school to address those “high risk” students.

[
269
]

Counsel for the plaintiffs urged me to find that
because Jeffrey had been teased and “victimized” at school, as had D.G., they
were at high risk of striking out at others. With respect, based on the
evidence presented, I cannot make that finding on the balance of probabilities.
There was no expert evidence presented from a psychologist or other qualified
behavioural expert who could give that opinion based on the records and perhaps
after intervening Jeffrey and/or D.G.. While Mr. Toll expressed the opinion
that they were “high risk” students, especially D.G., he was not qualified as
an expert to express that opinion. Absent an expert opinion, I find that the
school personnel were in the best position to make determinations regarding
“high risk” students.

[
270
]

Brockenshire J. reminded us in his thorough and
thoughtful decision in
Pellitteri
that the facts giving rise to an
action are not to be viewed through the clarifying lens of hindsight; they must
be viewed as they would have been seen before the accident and the resulting
injury.

[
271
]

Jeffrey and D.G. had special needs and while
they may have been “at risk” academically, their needs in that regard were
being addressed by the school in a caring and compassionate way. Their
behavioural issues as reflected in their incident reports and comments in their
IEPs were not such that one would have fact-based concerns about them being a
danger to themselves or others.

[
272
]

The one area of concern that I have in assessing
whether the school should have considered them “high risk” students needing a
higher level of supervision was the teasing to which both boys were subjected
to at school. The parents of both of the boys had spoken to the principal about
it. D.G. and Jeffrey along with their parents testified that the teasing upset
them. D.G. tried approaching his classmates in the classroom telling them how
much the teasing hurt him and asking them to stop. Jeffrey was also subjected
in the classroom to what could be considered physical intimidation. There was
an incident involving a protractor which I accept happened in some fashion.
Mrs. Mather-Breault did not recall it happening in her class but Mr. Power
acknowledged that he heard about it, probably from Mrs. Patrick and that he had
discussed it with Ms. Mather-Breault. While I find that the school did not deal
effectively with the teasing and what can only be called bullying especially as
it pertains to Jeffrey, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that
the proper solution was to provide a higher level of supervision of Jeffrey
while he was on the schoolyard. A review of the Violence Free School Policy
does not make any reference to such a procedure. The fact that no extra
supervision was provided, even though in hindsight it might have been helpful,
does not in itself breach the duty of care the school owed to Jeffrey. The
evidence does not support a finding that a higher level of supervision or a
direction to the schoolyard supervisor to keep an extra eye out for Jeffrey
would have prevented the incident. I find that it was a sudden, unexpected
event and the plaintiffs have not established otherwise on the balance of
probabilities. The action is therefore dismissed with costs to the defendants,
if sought.
